newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa sees delay in Zairean peace talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa sees delay in Zairean peace talks.

text.p: Last-minute haggling has delayed the first face-to-face encounter between Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and his civil war rival Laurent Kabila, South African government sources said on Monday.
But they said President Nelson Mandela telephoned Mobutu over the weekend and remained confident that talks to avert a rebel assault on Kinshasa would go ahead.
"The president is not despondent. He is confident that we will pull this thing off," one government source said.
"Both sides seem still to be committed to negotiations to prevent any escalation of the conflict in Zaire...to avert the risk of bloodshed that would go with an assault on Kinshasa."
South African officials had tentatively scheduled the talks for Wednesday in Cape Town, where Mandela last week brokered an agreement between the government and the rebels to meet.

But government sources said the informal timetable had slipped and there was no immediate indication of when Mobutu might meet Kabila, whose rebel alliance has seized control of about half of Zaire, including its mines.
The South African sources said Mobutu had yet to respond formally to Mandela's written invitation last week to a meeting with Kabila.

The sources cited different reasons for the slippage on a date for a meeting, with one citing efforts by other governments to become involved and another saying there was uncertainty about the agenda for the first meeting.
Mobutu's son and spokesman, Nganza Mobutu, said last week his ailing father, who has governed for 32 years, would meet Kabila to discuss election plans, but not his resignation.
Kabila appeared to raise the stakes after agreeing to talks, saying last week he was interested only in a ceremony to transfer power from Mobutu, 66, to his alliance.
Kabila, who is already granting mining concessions to Western companies in areas he controls, has vowed to take Kinshasa within three weeks if Mobutu does not agree to hand over power.

The sources said little was likely to be decided before Deputy President Thabo Mbeki returned on Wednesday from Washington, where he is discussing bilateral issues and the Zaire peace initiative with Vice President Al Gore and U.S. government officials.

Mbeki has so far handled the details of the South African peace initiative launched earlier this year by Mandela, who said last week the key to peace could be an arrangement for Mobutu to "go with dignity".
